label: Species are not immutable but descend from other, mostly extinct, species
claim: Species are not independently created and immutable; species of the same genus are lineal descendants of some other, generally extinct, species, just as varieties of one species descend from that species.
quote: I am fully convinced that species are not immutable; but that those belonging to what are called the same genera are lineal descendants of some other and generally extinct species, in the same manner as the acknowledged varieties of any one species are the descendants of that species.
scope: all species of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic relatedness of congeneric species
presence of extinct ancestral or stem taxa in the fossil record
candidate_data: Molecular phylogenies and divergence times (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree, GenBank) combined with fossil occurrences (Paleobiology Database).

label: Natural selection is the main but not exclusive means of modification
claim: Natural selection has been the main, but not the only, cause of the modification of species.
quote: Furthermore, I am convinced that Natural Selection has been the main but not exclusive means of modification.
measurable_quantities: proportion of phenotypic or sequence divergence attributable to selection versus other processes
strength of selection on traits in wild populations
candidate_data: Compilations of selection gradients in wild populations, genome-wide scans for selection in GenBank/SRA data, and experimental-evolution results such as the LTEE.

label: Overproduction plus slight profitable variation leads to natural selection
claim: Because more individuals of each species are born than can survive, there is a recurring struggle for existence, so any individual that varies even slightly in a way profitable to itself has a better chance of surviving and thus of being naturally selected.
quote: As many more individuals of each species are born than can possibly survive; and as, consequently, there is a frequently recurring struggle for existence, it follows that any being, if it vary however slightly in any manner profitable to itself, under the complex and sometimes varying conditions of life, will have a better chance of surviving, and thus be _naturally selected_.
measurable_quantities: offspring produced versus offspring surviving to reproduce
association between heritable trait values and survival or reproductive success
candidate_data: Life-table and demographic data (COMADRE, COMPADRE), long-term individual-based field studies of selection, and experimental-evolution datasets such as the LTEE.

label: External conditions alone cannot explain complex coadaptations
claim: Complex adaptations and coadaptations between organisms, such as the woodpecker's feeding structures or the misseltoe's dependence on particular trees, birds and insects, cannot be accounted for by the direct effects of external conditions such as climate and food.
quote: it is preposterous to attribute to mere external conditions, the structure, for instance, of the woodpecker, with its feet, tail, beak, and tongue, so admirably adapted to catch insects under the bark of trees.
scope: adapted structures of animals and plants, especially those involving relations with other species
measurable_quantities: magnitude of phenotypic plasticity induced by environment versus heritable trait differences
degree of trait matching between interacting species
candidate_data: Common-garden and reciprocal-transplant studies of plasticity versus heritable divergence; interaction-network data such as the Web of Life database.

label: Natural selection causes extinction of less improved forms and divergence
claim: Natural selection almost inevitably causes much extinction of less improved forms of life and produces divergence of character.
quote: we shall then see how Natural Selection almost inevitably causes much Extinction of the less improved forms of life and induces what I have called Divergence of Character.
scope: all organic beings over evolutionary time
measurable_quantities: extinction rates of lineages
morphological disparity among descendant lineages over time
candidate_data: Fossil occurrence and extinction data (Paleobiology Database) and time-calibrated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) with trait data.

label: Domesticated forms vary more among individuals than wild species do
claim: Individuals of the same variety of long-cultivated plants and domesticated animals generally differ much more from each other than individuals of any one species or variety in nature.
quote: they generally differ much more from each other, than do the individuals of any one species or variety in a state of nature.
scope: older cultivated plants and domesticated animals compared with wild species
measurable_quantities: within-breed or within-variety phenotypic variance
within-population phenotypic variance in wild relatives
candidate_data: Morphometric and trait datasets for breeds and their wild progenitors (e.g. TRY plant trait database for crops and wild relatives) and genomic variation data in GenBank/SRA.

label: Greater domestic variability is caused by changed, less uniform conditions
claim: The greater variability of domestic productions is due to their being raised under conditions of life less uniform than, and somewhat different from, those of their parent species in nature.
quote: I think we are driven to conclude that this greater variability is simply due to our domestic productions having been raised under conditions of life not so uniform as, and somewhat different from, those to which the parent-species have been exposed under nature.
measurable_quantities: phenotypic variance of populations raised under novel versus ancestral conditions
heritable variance generated per generation under changed conditions
candidate_data: Experimental-evolution and stress-induced variation studies (e.g. Dryad experimental-evolution datasets) and common-garden comparisons of crops and wild relatives.

label: Variability arises mainly from effects on reproductive elements before conception
claim: The most frequent cause of variability is that the male and female reproductive elements have been affected by the conditions of life before conception, the reproductive system being more sensitive to changed conditions than any other part of the organisation.
quote: But I am strongly inclined to suspect that the most frequent cause of variability may be attributed to the male and female reproductive elements having been affected prior to the act of conception.
scope: animals and plants under domestication or confinement
measurable_quantities: offspring variance as a function of parental environmental exposure before conception
fertility under confinement or cultivation
candidate_data: Parental-environment and germline mutation-rate studies with sequencing data in GenBank/SRA; zoo breeding records such as those in ZIMS (Species360).

label: Inherited effects of use and disuse modify domestic animals
claim: Habitual use and disuse of parts produce inherited changes in domestic animals; for example, domestic ducks have lighter wing bones and heavier leg bones relative to the skeleton than wild ducks because they fly less and walk more.
quote: I find in the domestic duck that the bones of the wing weigh less and the bones of the leg more, in proportion to the whole skeleton, than do the same bones in the wild-duck; and I presume that this change may be safely attributed to the domestic duck flying much less, and walking more, than its wild parent.
measurable_quantities: relative wing and leg bone mass in domestic versus wild ducks
trait differences in offspring of exercised versus unexercised parents
candidate_data: Museum osteological collections (e.g. records accessible via GBIF and VertNet) for the morphological pattern; transgenerational experiments for the claimed cause.

label: Selecting one trait unconsciously modifies other correlated parts
claim: Because of laws of correlation of growth, when man selects for and augments any peculiarity, he almost certainly also modifies other parts of the structure without intending to.
quote: Hence, if man goes on selecting, and thus augmenting, any peculiarity, he will almost certainly unconsciously modify other parts of the structure, owing to the mysterious laws of the correlation of growth.
scope: domesticated animals and cultivated plants under artificial selection
measurable_quantities: correlated responses of unselected traits in selection experiments
genetic correlations between traits
candidate_data: Artificial-selection experiment datasets (e.g. the Illinois long-term maize selection experiment, mouse and Drosophila selection lines on Dryad) and AnimalQTLdb.

label: Inherited peculiarities appear in offspring at the age they appeared in parent
claim: A peculiarity tends to appear in the offspring at the same period of life at which it first appeared in the parent, though sometimes earlier.
quote: A much more important rule, which I think may be trusted, is that, at whatever period of life a peculiarity first appears, it tends to appear in the offspring at a corresponding age, though sometimes earlier.
scope: domesticated animals and plants, extended to organisms generally
measurable_quantities: age of onset of heritable traits or diseases in parents and offspring
candidate_data: Pedigree databases of age of onset for heritable conditions, e.g. OMIA (Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals) and OMIM.

label: Domestic races differ like congeneric species, but usually less
claim: Apart from their lesser uniformity, their often monstrous development of one part, and their fertility when crossed, domestic races of a species differ from each other in the same manner as closely allied species of a genus in nature, though in most cases to a lesser degree.
quote: domestic races of the same species differ from each other in the same manner as, only in most cases in a lesser degree than, do closely-allied species of the same genus in a state of nature.
scope: domestic races compared with closely allied wild congeneric species
measurable_quantities: morphological distance between breeds of one species
morphological distance between congeneric wild species
candidate_data: Morphometric datasets of breeds (e.g. dog and pigeon skull morphometrics on Dryad) compared with wild-species trait data from museum collections accessible via GBIF.

section: Origin of Domestic Varieties from one or more Species
label: Any wild species domesticated as long would vary as much as existing domestics
claim: Domesticated species were not chosen for an unusual inherent tendency to vary; any comparable set of wild animals and plants, bred under domestication for as many generations, would on average vary as much as the parent species of existing domesticated productions have.
quote: I cannot doubt that if other animals and plants, equal in number to our domesticated productions, and belonging to equally diverse classes and countries, were taken from a state of nature, and could be made to breed for an equal number of generations under domestication, they would vary on an average as largely as the parent species of our existing domesticated productions have varied.
scope: wild animals and plants brought into domestication
measurable_quantities: standing genetic and phenotypic variation in domesticated progenitors versus non-domesticated relatives
rate of phenotypic diversification under captive breeding
candidate_data: Long-term captive-domestication experiments (e.g. the Novosibirsk farm-fox experiment) and genomic diversity data for wild species in GenBank/SRA.

section: Origin of Domestic Varieties from one or more Species
label: Domestic dogs descend from several wild species
claim: Domestic dogs have probably descended from several distinct wild species rather than from a single one.
quote: from geographical and other considerations, I think it highly probable that our domestic dogs have descended from several wild species.
measurable_quantities: genomic ancestry proportions of dog breeds from wild canid species
phylogenetic placement of dogs among Canidae
candidate_data: Modern and ancient canid genome sequences in GenBank/SRA and the European Nucleotide Archive.

section: Domestic Pigeons, their Differences and Origin
label: All domestic pigeon breeds descend from the rock-pigeon
claim: All domestic pigeon breeds, however different, have descended from the rock-pigeon (Columba livia) and its geographical sub-species, not from several aboriginal wild stocks.
quote: I can feel no doubt that all our domestic breeds have descended from the Columba livia with its geographical sub-species.
measurable_quantities: genomic ancestry of pigeon breeds
phylogenetic relationships of breeds to wild Columba species
candidate_data: Whole-genome resequencing data for pigeon breeds and wild Columba in GenBank/SRA.

section: Principle of Selection anciently followed, its Effects
label: Domestic breeds arise mainly by man's accumulation of successive variations
claim: Domestic breeds were not produced suddenly in their present useful form; their key cause is man's accumulative selection, nature supplying successive variations and man adding them up in directions useful to him.
quote: The key is man’s power of accumulative selection: nature gives successive variations; man adds them up in certain directions useful to him.
measurable_quantities: cumulative response to selection over generations
historical trait trajectories of breeds and cultivars
candidate_data: Long-term artificial-selection experiments (e.g. the Illinois long-term maize selection experiment) and breed-history genomic data in GenBank/SRA.

section: Principle of Selection anciently followed, its Effects
label: Races differ most in the parts man selects
claim: Continued selection of slight variations in one part valued by man, such as leaves, flowers or fruit, produces races that differ from each other chiefly in that part, while other parts differ only slightly.
quote: as a general rule, I cannot doubt that the continued selection of slight variations, either in the leaves, the flowers, or the fruit, will produce races differing from each other chiefly in these characters.
scope: cultivated plant varieties within a species
measurable_quantities: among-variety variance in the selected organ
among-variety variance in unselected organs
candidate_data: Crop germplasm trait records (e.g. USDA GRIN-Global germplasm evaluation data) and TRY plant trait database.

label: Unconscious selection over centuries modifies any breed
claim: Unconscious selection, in which people simply breed from their best animals without aiming to change the breed, would over centuries improve and modify any breed, as methodical breeders have done within their lifetimes.
quote: Nevertheless I cannot doubt that this process, continued during centuries, would improve and modify any breed, in the same way as Bakewell, Collins, etc., by this very same process, only carried on more methodically, did greatly modify, even during their own lifetimes, the forms and qualities of their cattle.
measurable_quantities: change in breed traits over historical time
trait differences between historical and modern specimens of a breed
candidate_data: Ancient-DNA and archaeozoological time series of domestic animals and crops, and historical breed-standard morphometrics.

label: Domestic races differ greatly externally but little internally
claim: Because man can select mainly on externally visible deviations, domestic races differ greatly in external characters and relatively slightly in internal parts or organs.
quote: We can, I think, further understand the frequently abnormal character of our domestic races, and likewise their differences being so great in external characters and relatively so slight in internal parts or organs.
measurable_quantities: among-breed variance in external traits
among-breed variance in internal organ size and structure
candidate_data: Breed morphometric and anatomical datasets (e.g. dog and chicken breed studies on Dryad) and AnimalQTLdb trait records.

section: Unknown Origin of our Domestic Productions
label: Slow accumulated change hides the wild parents of old cultivated plants
claim: Because a large amount of change has been slowly and unconsciously accumulated in long-cultivated plants, in many cases their wild parent-stocks can no longer be recognised.
quote: A large amount of change in our cultivated plants, thus slowly and unconsciously accumulated, explains, as I believe, the well-known fact, that in a vast number of cases we cannot recognise, and therefore do not know, the wild parent-stocks of the plants which have been longest cultivated in our flower and kitchen gardens.
measurable_quantities: morphological divergence of crops from wild progenitors
duration of cultivation
candidate_data: Crop wild relative inventories and phylogenomic data on crop origins (GenBank/SRA, Crop Wild Relatives inventory of the Crop Trust), with archaeobotanical dates.

section: Circumstances favourable to Man’s power of Selection
label: Keeping large numbers of individuals favours successful selection
claim: Because useful variations appear only occasionally, keeping a large number of individuals greatly increases the chance of useful variations appearing and is of the highest importance to success in selection.
quote: But as variations manifestly useful or pleasing to man appear only occasionally, the chance of their appearance will be much increased by a large number of individuals being kept; and hence this comes to be of the highest importance to success.
scope: artificial selection on domesticated animals and plants
measurable_quantities: response to selection as a function of population size
number of novel variants per generation versus population size
candidate_data: Selection experiments varying population size (Drosophila and mouse selection lines on Dryad) and experimental-evolution data such as the LTEE.

label: Accumulative selection is the predominant cause of change in domestic races
claim: Among the causes of change in domestic races, including conditions of life, use and disuse, correlation and crossing, the accumulative action of selection, whether methodical or unconscious, is by far the predominant power.
quote: Over all these causes of Change I am convinced that the accumulative action of Selection, whether applied methodically and more quickly, or unconsciously and more slowly, but more efficiently, is by far the predominant Power.
measurable_quantities: fraction of breed differentiation attributable to selection versus drift, admixture or plasticity
candidate_data: Genome-wide selection scans and admixture analyses of breeds and crops using GenBank/SRA data.

label: Individual differences supply the material for natural selection
claim: The slight individual differences among members of a species provide the materials that natural selection accumulates, in the same way that man accumulates individual differences in domestic productions.
quote: These individual differences are highly important for us, as they afford materials for natural selection to accumulate, in the same manner as man can accumulate in any given direction individual differences in his domesticated productions.
scope: species in a state of nature
measurable_quantities: heritability of individual trait differences in wild populations
response to natural selection in wild populations
candidate_data: Long-term wild pedigree studies and compilations of heritability and selection estimates; experimental-evolution datasets on Dryad.

label: Polymorphic genera vary in traits of no use, unfixed by selection
claim: In polymorphic genera such as Rubus, Rosa and Hieracium, the inordinate variation concerns structures that are of no service or disservice to the species and so have not been seized on and made definite by natural selection.
quote: I am inclined to suspect that we see in these polymorphic genera variations in points of structure which are of no service or disservice to the species, and which consequently have not been seized on and rendered definite by natural selection
scope: polymorphic genera of plants, insects and brachiopods
measurable_quantities: fitness effects of the variable characters
within-genus variability of characters compared with non-polymorphic genera
candidate_data: Taxonomic and trait data for apomictic plant complexes (World Flora Online, TRY plant trait database) with field fitness measurements.

label: No clear line separates species, sub-species, varieties and individual differences
claim: No clear line of demarcation exists between species and sub-species, between sub-species and well-marked varieties, or between lesser varieties and individual differences; they blend into one another in an insensible series.
quote: Certainly no clear line of demarcation has as yet been drawn between species and sub-species—that is, the forms which in the opinion of some naturalists come very near to, but do not quite arrive at the rank of species; or, again, between sub-species and well-marked varieties, or between lesser varieties and individual differences.
measurable_quantities: distribution of genetic or morphological distances among infraspecific and interspecific pairs
frequency of taxonomic disagreement over rank
candidate_data: Sequence divergence data such as DNA barcodes in BOLD and GenBank, and taxonomic checklists with infraspecific ranks (WCVP, Catalogue of Life).

label: Doubtful forms of mobile animals are rare within a country but common between areas
claim: Among highly locomotive animals that unite for each birth, doubtful forms ranked as species by some and varieties by others are rarely found within the same country but are common in separated areas.
quote: Amongst animals which unite for each birth, and which are highly locomotive, doubtful forms, ranked by one zoologist as a species and by another as a variety, can rarely be found within the same country, but are common in separated areas.
scope: highly mobile sexually reproducing animals such as birds and insects
measurable_quantities: number of contested species/subspecies pairs that are sympatric versus allopatric
candidate_data: Comparison of differing taxonomies (e.g. Clements/eBird, IOC World Bird List, HBW and BirdLife checklists) with range maps from BirdLife International and GBIF occurrences.

label: Natural selection turns slight varieties into more distinct ones and species
claim: Individual differences lead to slight varieties, these to more distinct and permanent varieties, then to sub-species and species, the passage being mainly due to natural selection accumulating structural differences in definite directions, so that a well-marked variety is an incipient species.
quote: I attribute the passage of a variety, from a state in which it differs very slightly from its parent to one in which it differs more, to the action of natural selection in accumulating (as will hereafter be more fully explained) differences of structure in certain definite directions.
measurable_quantities: divergence between incipient species over time
signatures of divergent selection between populations
candidate_data: Population-genomic data for speciation continua in GenBank/SRA and divergence-time estimates in TimeTree.

label: The term species is arbitrary and not essentially different from variety
claim: The term species is given arbitrarily, for convenience, to a set of closely resembling individuals and does not differ essentially from the term variety, which is given to less distinct and more fluctuating forms.
quote: I look at the term species, as one arbitrarily given for the sake of convenience to a set of individuals closely resembling each other, and that it does not essentially differ from the term variety, which is given to less distinct and more fluctuating forms.
candidate_data: none known

section: Wide ranging, much diffused, and common species vary most
label: Dominant species, widespread and abundant, produce the most varieties
claim: The dominant species, those that range widely over the world, are most diffused in their own country and are most numerous in individuals, most often produce well-marked varieties.
quote: Hence it is the most flourishing, or, as they may be called, the dominant species,—those which range widely over the world, are the most diffused in their own country, and are the most numerous in individuals,—which oftenest produce well-marked varieties, or, as I consider them, incipient species.
measurable_quantities: number of recorded varieties or subspecies per species
geographic range size
local abundance or occupancy
candidate_data: Infraspecific taxon counts from the World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP) or POWO combined with range and occurrence data from GBIF.

section: Species of the larger genera in any country vary more than the species of the smaller genera
label: Species of larger genera more often present varieties
claim: Within a country, a larger proportion of the species in larger genera present varieties than of the species in smaller genera, and those that vary have on average more varieties.
quote: it has invariably proved to be the case that a larger proportion of the species on the side of the larger genera present varieties, than on the side of the smaller genera.
scope: plants of regional floras and beetles of local faunas
measurable_quantities: proportion of species with recorded varieties by genus size
mean number of varieties per varying species by genus size
candidate_data: Genus sizes and infraspecific taxa from the World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP) or regional floras, and the Catalogue of Life for beetles.

section: Species of the larger genera in any country vary more than the species of the smaller genera
label: Where many species of a genus have formed, many are still forming
claim: On the view that species are strongly marked varieties, where many species of a genus have been formed, on average many new species should still be forming.
quote: All that we want to show is, that where many species of a genus have been formed, on an average many are still forming; and this holds good.
measurable_quantities: recent speciation rate per clade
clade species richness
candidate_data: Time-calibrated phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree) for estimating tip speciation rates against clade richness.

section: Species of the larger genera in any country vary more than the species of the smaller genera
label: Small genera often grow large while large genera peak, decline and vanish
claim: Over geological time small genera have often increased greatly in number of species, and large genera have often reached a maximum, declined and disappeared.
quote: geology plainly tells us that small genera have in the lapse of time often increased greatly in size; and that large genera have often come to their maxima, declined, and disappeared.
measurable_quantities: species richness of genera through time
genus duration and trajectory of richness before extinction
candidate_data: Fossil occurrence data from the Paleobiology Database.

section: Many of the species of the larger genera resemble varieties in being very closely, but unequally, related to each other, and in having restricted ranges
label: Species in large genera differ from one another by small amounts
claim: In large genera the amount of difference between species is often exceedingly small, so that their species resemble varieties more than do species of small genera.
quote: Now Fries has remarked in regard to plants, and Westwood in regard to insects, that in large genera the amount of difference between the species is often exceedingly small. I have endeavoured to test this numerically by averages, and, as far as my imperfect results go, they always confirm the view.
measurable_quantities: mean pairwise morphological or genetic distance among congeners as a function of genus size
candidate_data: Sequence data (GenBank, BOLD) and trait data (TRY plant trait database) analysed against genus sizes from WCVP or Catalogue of Life.

section: Many of the species of the larger genera resemble varieties in being very closely, but unequally, related to each other, and in having restricted ranges
label: Species of large genera cluster unequally around certain species
claim: Species of large genera are not equally distinct from one another but are clustered in little groups around certain other species, as varieties are clustered around their parent species.
quote: As Fries has well remarked, little groups of species are generally clustered like satellites around certain other species.
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic tree balance and clustering of species within genera
variance of pairwise distances among congeners
candidate_data: Species-level phylogenies from Open Tree of Life and TimeTree, and GenBank sequence data.

section: Many of the species of the larger genera resemble varieties in being very closely, but unequally, related to each other, and in having restricted ranges
label: Species very closely allied to others have restricted ranges, like varieties
claim: Species that are very closely allied to other species, and so resemble varieties, often have much restricted ranges, similar to the restricted ranges of acknowledged varieties.
quote: But there is also reason to believe, that those species which are very closely allied to other species, and in so far resemble varieties, often have much restricted ranges.
scope: plants (British flora), extended to species generally
measurable_quantities: range size of species as a function of genetic or morphological distance to nearest relative
range size of varieties versus their parent species
candidate_data: Occurrence data from GBIF and range maps combined with phylogenies from Open Tree of Life or GenBank sequence data.

label: Analogies between species of large genera and varieties support descent
claim: The analogies between species of large genera and varieties (more varieties, small and unequal differences, restricted ranges) are understandable if species once existed as varieties, and inexplicable if each species was independently created.
quote: And we can clearly understand these analogies, if species have once existed as varieties, and have thus originated: whereas, these analogies are utterly inexplicable if each species has been independently created.
scope: species and varieties of plants and animals
candidate_data: none known

label: Larger genera tend to grow larger and dominant forms more dominant
claim: Because the dominant species of larger genera vary most and varieties become new species, larger genera tend to become larger, and dominant forms tend to become more dominant by leaving many modified, dominant descendants.
quote: The larger genera thus tend to become larger; and throughout nature the forms of life which are now dominant tend to become still more dominant by leaving many modified and dominant descendants.
scope: genera and dominant species throughout nature
measurable_quantities: correlation between clade size and diversification rate
number of descendant species from widespread versus restricted ancestors
candidate_data: Time-calibrated phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree) and fossil genus richness trajectories in the Paleobiology Database.
